messages.subject: Predicting with 'State'
parts:
Hello,

I am attempting to predict abundance for unmarked animals throughout multiple sites that have been surveyed multiple times. In my binomial mixture model, I have several detection and abundance covariates. When I predict 'state', how are my detection covariates influencing my predictions of abundance? Do I need to set my detection covariates to their mean before predicting or do I not need to worry about that? I am looking to predict abundance, based mostly on landcover classification, into unsurveyed areas and am unsure of how my detection covariates will influence these predictions.
Any input would be apreciated.

Thank you,
Sarah

#best ranked model
model.1=pcount(~date+dist.trav+weather~-1+PC1+PC2+PC3+DTC,snail.umf.pc,mixture='NB')
#prediction
Full.Predict=predict(model.1,newdata=newdata9,type='state',appendData=T); Full.Predict

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Predicting with 'State'
parts:
If you are interested in predicting abundance, then you want those predictions based only on the abundance predictors.  pcount (and other routines in unmarked) allow one to get estimates "free and clear" of the nuisance caused by less-than-perfect detection.  While the detection parameters certainly influence the observed counts, the predictions are about what one would observe if detection was perfect.  Now if the detection probabilities are low that that will generally increase the standard errors for the estimates of abundance and the associated parameters.  So there is an influence in that respect.

Sometimes one is also interested in the detection part of the model to ascertain what factors influence detection probabilities and what one might want to do when designing future surveys.

And I might likely be in the minority here but if PC1+PC2+PC3 means the first three principal components of some set of environmental variables, then unless you have a solid interpretation for each component, I'd avoid using those.  Performing manipulations on a large set of variables in complete isolation of what one wants to predict makes little sense to me.  Yes, the principal components are orthogonal to each other (by definition) but there's no reason to believe that the top 3 principal components will be good predictors or better than any of the remaining principal components.

Jim

Jim

messages.author: 9a9d77f92ad5e6da
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Predicting with 'State'
parts:
Thank you for your response Jim. Your explanation was very helpful. 

The PCs do mean the first 3 principle components. I am working in wetlands throughout Florida and originally my dataset included over 40 different landcover classifications, many of which were only used a handful of times but explained specific wetlands. I used a PCA to determine which wetland classifications explained the most variation. The first 3 PCs correspond to 4 common and biologically important wetland classifications and explained close to 80% of the variation in my data. I am attempting to predict based on the proportion of each PC within each surveyed site. I used a PCA because my model originally wouldn't run with so many abundance covariates and I needed a repeatable way to reduce landcover classifications. Do you know of any way to do so without using a PCA?

Best,
Sarah

messages.author: 247b990d236a7af6
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Predicting with 'State'
parts:
If you're wanting to predict abundance (as opposed to understand the underlying mechanisms of abundance, i.e., "interpreting coefficients"), then using principal components is fine as long as the prediction intervals meet your desired levels of precision.

If "explaining" predictions is the objective, then using principal components or throwing out highly correlated predictors just hides the multicollinearity issue.  "Explaining" needs lots of thinking and subject matter knowledge and automatic processes such as principal components tends to bypass the thinking and subject matter knowledge components.  (If all it took was a numeric procedure, why would we statisticians need you guys?)

Things are not certainly as black-and-white as maybe I've implied above, but if prediction is the objective, then you're not as restricted to what you can do and in the end, good enough predictions are what counts.  (Assuming one knows what "good enough" is.)

Jim
